## The Analytic Question

### Our research question

| Do patients on treatment differ from those not on treatment?
| Which characteristics (age, sex, comorbidity) differ between the two groups?

### Define the analytic population FIRST

| Uptake only makes sense for those already diagnosed.
| We restrict to htn\_diagnosed == "Yes" (about 1,089 patients).
| Roughly 47% of diagnosed patients had taken up treatment.

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not analyse all 1,500
Including undiagnosed people, whose outcome is undefined, biases every result.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: define the analytic population explicitly and once, before any test.

Clinical logic: you cannot take up treatment for a disease you have not been diagnosed with.

Common mistake: running the analysis on the full 1,500 - it mixes in undefined outcomes and biases estimates.

Demo tip: show dx \<- filter(analysis\_data, htn\_diagnosed == "Yes") then nrow(dx) and table(dx\$treatment\_uptake).
:::

## Hypothesis Testing in Plain Language

### The two hypotheses

| Null (H0): there is NO difference / NO association.
| Alternative (H1): there IS a difference / association.

### What a p-value actually is

| The probability of data this extreme IF the null were true.
| Small p (\< 0.05) is evidence AGAINST the null.
| It is NOT the probability that the null is true.

::: {.callout-note}
## Significance level
We pre-set alpha = 0.05 as the threshold for calling a result significant.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: a p-value answers 'how surprising is my data if nothing is going on?'

Common misinterpretation: p is NOT the chance the null is true, and (1 - p) is NOT the chance H1 is true.

Clinical interpretation: significance is about evidence against H0, not about importance or effect size.

Audience question: does p = 0.04 prove the effect is real? Answer: no - it is one piece of evidence, judged with the effect size and context.
:::

## p \< 0.05 Is Not the Whole Story

### Statistical vs clinical significance

| A tiny, meaningless difference can be 'significant' in a large sample.
| A large, important difference can be 'non-significant' if the sample is small.
| Always report the effect size and its confidence interval, not just p.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Beware p-value worship
Do not chase p \< 0.05 or treat 0.049 and 0.051 as opposites.

A confidence interval tells you the size AND the uncertainty.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: the p-value is necessary but not sufficient - it ignores effect size.

Common mistake: dichotomising at 0.05 as if 0.049 and 0.051 are fundamentally different.

Clinical interpretation: a CI shows both the magnitude and the precision; prefer it to a bare p-value.

Audience question: which is more useful, 'p = 0.03' or 'OR 3.6 (95% CI 1.5 to 9.6)'? Answer: the second - it shows direction, size and uncertainty.
:::

## Is the Variable Normal? Look, Then Test

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Look first (always)

- Histogram shows the shape of the distribution.
- Q-Q plot: points on the line means roughly normal.
- Points curving away at the ends mean skew or heavy tails.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Then test

- Shapiro-Wilk test: H0 is that data ARE normal.
- Small p (\< 0.05) means we reject normality.
- Symmetric and bell-shaped means a parametric test is fine.
- Clearly skewed means use the non-parametric test.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: plot before you test - the eye catches what a single p-value hides.

Common mistake: trusting Shapiro-Wilk alone in large samples; with \~1,089 rows it flags trivial departures as significant.

Clinical interpretation: a near-straight Q-Q plot and a symmetric histogram matter more than the Shapiro p here.

Demo tip: run hist(dx\$age), qqnorm/qqline, then shapiro.test(dx\$age) and contrast the verdicts.
:::

## Shapiro-Wilk: Use With Care in Big Samples

### Why the test misleads here

| Shapiro-Wilk gets more powerful as the sample grows.
| In \~1,089 rows it detects tiny, clinically irrelevant departures.
| It will almost always return p \< 0.05 - even for usable data.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb for this course
Big sample + symmetric histogram + straight Q-Q means parametric is fine.

Let the plots, not the Shapiro p-value, drive the decision.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: statistical power is a double-edged sword - in large n the normality test over-flags.

Common mistake: switching to non-parametric tests purely because Shapiro returned p \< 0.05.

Clinical interpretation: judge normality by shape and Q-Q linearity; reserve non-parametric tests for clear skew or small n.

Audience question: Shapiro says p \< 0.001 but the Q-Q is straight - what do you do? Answer: trust the plot and use the parametric test.
:::

## Comparing Two Groups: a Continuous Outcome

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### t-test (parametric)

- Compares MEANS of two groups.
- Welch t-test is the safe default (unequal variances).
- Use when data are roughly symmetric.
- Formula: age \~ treatment\_uptake.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Wilcoxon (non-parametric)

- Compares RANKS, not means.
- Robust to outliers and skew.
- Use when data are clearly non-normal.
- Report medians instead of means.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: the question is the same (do two groups differ?); the test depends on the data shape.

Clinical interpretation example: mean age is higher among those on treatment, consistent with older patients taking up more.

Common mistake: defaulting to the classic Student t-test - Welch is safer because it does not assume equal variances.

Demo tip: run both t.test and wilcox.test on age \~ treatment\_uptake; note they usually agree for large, symmetric data.
:::

## Demo: t-test of Age by Treatment Uptake

[Is mean age different between those who took up treatment and those who did not?]{.slide-intro}

```r
t.test(age ~ treatment_uptake, data = dx)
```

```{.text .code-output}
Welch Two Sample t-test
t = -8.9, df = 1011, p-value < 2.2e-16
95 percent CI: -6.4 to -4.1
mean in No  mean in Yes
   50.1        55.3
```

::: {.code-note}
Patients on treatment are about 5 years older on average; the CI excludes 0, so p \< 0.05.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: read three things - the two group means, the 95% CI for their difference, and the p-value.

Clinical interpretation: a \~5-year mean age gap, with a CI that excludes zero, supports older patients taking up more.

Common mistake: reporting only the p-value and omitting the means and the CI for the difference.

Demo tip: run wilcox.test(age \~ treatment\_uptake, data = dx) alongside and show they agree.
:::

## When Data Are Not Normal: Non-parametric Tests

### The rank-based alternatives

| Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney): compares two groups without assuming normality.
| Fisher's exact test: for a 2x2 table when expected counts are small (\< 5).
| They use ranks and exact counts instead of means and the normal curve.

### How to run them

| wilcox.test(sbp\_mmhg \~ treatment\_uptake, data = dx)
| fisher.test(table(dx\$treatment\_uptake, dx\$diabetes))

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
Skewed or small data -\> use the non-parametric test; it is the safe choice when in doubt.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: when the normality or sample-size assumptions of the t-test or chi-square fail, the rank-based Wilcoxon test and Fisher's exact test give valid answers.

Clinical interpretation: lab values and costs are often skewed - the Wilcoxon test on medians is frequently the honest choice.

Common mistake: forcing a t-test on clearly skewed data, or using chi-square when a cell has an expected count below 5.

Audience question: when would you prefer Fisher's exact over chi-square? Expected answer: small samples or sparse tables with low expected counts.

Demo tip: show that Wilcoxon and the t-test agree here (large, roughly symmetric sample), then contrive a small table to motivate Fisher's exact.
:::

## Comparing More Than Two Groups: ANOVA {.smaller}

### Why not many t-tests?

| Each pairwise t-test carries its own 5% false-positive risk.
| Doing several inflates the overall error rate.
| ANOVA tests all groups at once with one honest p-value.

### After a significant ANOVA

| A small p tells you SOME groups differ, not which ones.
| TukeyHSD compares every pair and corrects for multiplicity.
| Example: does age differ across education levels?

::: {.callout-note}
## If assumptions fail
Use the non-parametric kruskal.test() instead of aov().
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: ANOVA is the multi-group t-test; it controls the family-wide error a stack of t-tests would not.

Common mistake: running every pairwise t-test - inflates false positives. Run ANOVA, then a post-hoc only if it is significant.

Clinical interpretation: a Tukey table shows which specific education pairs differ in mean age.

Audience question: ANOVA p is significant - are all groups different? Answer: no, at least one pair is; Tukey says which.
:::

## Association Between Two Categories {.smaller}

### Chi-square test of independence

| Question: is treatment uptake associated with diabetes?
| Build a contingency table, then test it.
| H0: the two variables are independent (no association).

### When expected counts are small

| Chi-square needs all expected cell counts \>= 5.
| Check with chisq.test(tab)\$expected.
| If any are too small, use Fisher's exact test instead.

::: {.callout-note}
## The table gives direction
The test gives a p-value; the table shows WHO had higher uptake.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: chi-square asks whether two categorical variables move together; the table shows the direction.

Common mistake: applying chi-square when expected counts are below 5 - switch to Fisher's exact in that case.

Clinical interpretation: a higher proportion of diabetics on treatment suggests a positive association, quantified later by the OR.

Demo tip: show table(dx\$treatment\_uptake, dx\$diabetes), then chisq.test, its \$expected, and fisher.test.
:::

## Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Pearson

- Measures LINEAR association.
- Assumes roughly normal data.
- Sensitive to outliers.
- Example: sbp\_mmhg vs bmi.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Spearman

- Based on RANKS.
- Robust to outliers and non-linearity.
- Use when data are skewed.
- Reports a rank correlation.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: r ranges from -1 to +1; \~0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong; the sign gives direction.

Common mistake: confusing a significant p with a strong relationship - in big samples a tiny r (0.08) is significant yet trivial.

Clinical interpretation: always report and judge r, not just the p-value; remember correlation is not causation.

Audience question: r = 0.1, p \< 0.001 - strong link? Answer: no, statistically detectable but clinically negligible.
:::

## Demo: Correlation of SBP and BMI

[Do systolic blood pressure and BMI move together?]{.slide-intro}

```r
cor.test(dx$sbp_mmhg, dx$bmi, method = "pearson")
```

```{.text .code-output}
Pearson's product-moment correlation
t = 6.1, df = 1087, p-value = 1.4e-09
95 percent CI: 0.12 to 0.24
cor = 0.18
```

::: {.code-note}
r = 0.18 is a weak positive link: highly significant, but clinically modest.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: the p-value confirms the link is real; r tells you it is weak.

Clinical interpretation: SBP and BMI rise together a little, but BMI explains very little of SBP variation.

Common mistake: headlining 'significant correlation' while hiding that r is only 0.18.

Demo tip: rerun with method = "spearman" and note the rank correlation is similar, confirming robustness.
:::

## Choosing the Right Test

| Outcome | Predictor / 2nd variable | Test |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Continuous | Two groups | t-test (Wilcoxon if skewed) |
| Continuous | More than two groups | ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if skewed) |
| Categorical | Categorical | Chi-square (Fisher if sparse) |
| Continuous | Continuous | Correlation (Pearson / Spearman) |
| Binary | One or more predictors | Logistic regression - Day 5 |

: Match the QUESTION and the data types to the test; a binary outcome with predictors leads to regression (Day 5).

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: the test is determined by the outcome type and the predictor type - not by habit.

Demo tip: keep this table on screen as a decision aid for the exercise.

Clinical interpretation: when the outcome is binary and we want several predictors at once, we move to logistic regression - that is Day 5.

Audience question: outcome is Yes/No and we want to adjust for several factors - which method? Answer: logistic regression, next session.
:::

## Day 4 Exercise: Choose and Run the Right Test {.smaller}

### Your tasks

| Compare age between treatment-uptake groups with a t-test.
| Test the association between sex and treatment uptake (chi-square).
| Test the correlation between SBP and BMI (Pearson or Spearman).
| For each, state the question, the test, and a plain-language result.

### Expected output

| One test result per question, each with a p-value.
| For the t-test and correlation, the estimate and its 95% CI.
| One sentence interpreting each result clinically.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Let the data type choose the test
Check the outcome type and the number of groups before you pick a test.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key teaching point: the deliverable is the reasoning - question -\> variable types -\> test -\> interpretation.

Common mistake: reaching for a t-test out of habit without checking the outcome type or distribution.

Clinical interpretation: expect the SBP-BMI correlation to be weak but significant; sex-uptake association may be modest.

Demo tip: circulate and check that students report the estimate and CI, not just the p-value.
:::
